planting.note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Chinese woodland groundcover spreads by creeping stolons and forms a dense mat wherever soil stays reliably damp.

directions: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Chinese woodland groundcover spreads steadily by creeping stolons and forms a dense mat wherever soil stays reliably damp. Chrysosplenium davidianum is a low, spreading perennial native to moist forest floors and streamside rocks in central China, with small rounded, scalloped leaves and clusters of tiny chartreuse flowers backed by broad, colorful bracts that flush pink to bronze in cool weather, giving the plant a longer season of visual interest than most of its relatives. It has become a favorite of collectors for shaded rock gardens and moist woodland borders, where its vigorous mat-forming habit quickly covers bare ground between larger shade perennials. Divide congested patches every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and to share starts, since named color forms rarely come true from seed.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into permanently damp, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along stream edges, seeps, or bog gardens; opposite-leaved golden saxifrage needs constant moisture and spreads quickly into a low, mossy carpet once established.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into permanently damp, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along stream edges, seeps, or the muddy margins of a garden pond; opposite-leaved golden saxifrage spreads quickly by shallow, rooting stems into a low, mossy carpet wherever moisture is constant. Chrysosplenium oppositifolium is a creeping European and western Asian native common along shaded brooks and wet woodland flushes, with small, rounded, opposite leaves and flat clusters of minute, star-shaped, greenish-yellow flowers surrounded by yellow-green bracts in early spring that give the plant its glowing common name from a distance. It is among the most vigorous species in the genus, readily filling damp shaded gaps where turf and most other groundcovers fail, and is a traditional companion to ferns and mosses in British and continental European stream and bog gardens. It can become locally aggressive in ideal boggy conditions, so site it where its spread is welcome or contained by a path or stone edging.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under conifers or along streambanks; Brewer's mitrewort resents summer heat and dry soil and performs best in the cool, moist forests of its native Pacific Northwest range.

directions: Plant divisions in early spring into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade under conifers, along streambanks, or in a shaded rock garden; Brewer's mitrewort resents summer heat and dry soil and performs best where the Pacific Northwest's cool, moist forest conditions can be approximated. Mitella breweri forms low rosettes of rounded, softly hairy, heart-shaped leaves from which slender, leafless flower stalks rise in late spring, bearing a one-sided raceme of tiny greenish flowers whose petals are so finely dissected they resemble miniature snowflakes under magnification. Native to moist coniferous forests and subalpine meadows from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Olympics, it is a quiet, textural addition to a native shade garden, best massed with ferns and other small woodlanders where its intricate flowers can be appreciated up close. Divide congested clumps in spring, since seed germination is slow and often erratic.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade beneath conifers or broadleaf trees; oval-leaved miterwort naturalizes along shaded stream terraces and forest floors from coastal redwood groves to the Cascades.

directions: Plant divisions in early spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade beneath conifers or broadleaf trees; oval-leaved miterwort forms spreading colonies along shaded stream terraces and forest floors from the coastal redwood belt north into the Cascades and Olympic Mountains. Its rounded to oval, scalloped basal leaves stay attractive through the growing season, and in spring, wiry, leafless stalks carry small racemes of tiny greenish-white, fringed flowers typical of the genus, best appreciated at close range along a shaded path or in a woodland rock garden. It tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil moisture than other native mitreworts, making it a dependable, low-maintenance companion to sword fern, redwood sorrel, and other Pacific Coast forest understory plants. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along streambanks or seepage slopes; leafy-stemmed miterwort needs steady moisture and cool root conditions to thrive.

directions: Plant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along streambanks, seeps, or moist forest ravines; leafy-stemmed miterwort needs steady moisture and cool root conditions to thrive and will not tolerate summer drought. Unlike most miterworts, Mitella caulescens carries a pair of small leaves partway up its otherwise leafless flowering stem, above which opens a loose raceme of distinctive flowers with delicate, reddish-tinged, deeply fringed petals that give the plant a subtly showier presence than its relatives. Native to moist coniferous forests from British Columbia south through the Cascades and Coast Ranges to northern California, it is prized by native plant collectors for shaded stream gardens where its fine-textured foliage and intricate blooms can be viewed up close. Divide established clumps in spring to propagate, since seed can be slow and irregular to germinate.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along mountain streambanks or in a shaded scree bed; five-point bishop's cap is adapted to cool subalpine conditions and struggles in hot, humid summer climates.

directions: Plant divisions in early spring into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along mountain streambanks, seeps, or a shaded scree bed; five-point bishop's cap is adapted to cool subalpine conditions and struggles wherever summers are hot and humid. Mitella pentandra is a wide-ranging western North American native found from Alaska south through the Rocky Mountains and Cascades into the high Sierra Nevada, forming compact rosettes of small, glossy, kidney-shaped leaves beneath slender racemes of tiny, five-parted, greenish-yellow flowers with delicately fringed petals in early to mid-summer. It is best suited to cool-summer rock gardens, alpine troughs, or the shaded margins of a mountain-style water feature, where its diminutive scale and finely wrought blooms reward close inspection. Divide established clumps in spring for propagation, as seed is slow to germinate and best sown fresh.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees; Large Toothwort is an uncommon eastern woodland ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbance.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees; Large Toothwort is an uncommon eastern North American spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location carefully to avoid disturbing the rhizomes during summer garden work. Cardamine maxima produces broad, coarsely toothed leaves arranged in a distinctive whorl partway up the stem, larger and more robust than those of the more common cutleaf and Douglass's toothworts, topped in early spring with loose clusters of white to pale pink four-petaled flowers. Found scattered through rich cove forests and calcareous woodlands from New England south through the Appalachians, it is genuinely rare in cultivation and a worthwhile addition for collectors building out a full sequence of native toothworts alongside trout lily and bloodroot. Divide clumps carefully in fall once foliage has withered, since the brittle rhizomes are easily damaged.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or fall-sown seed in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade under oaks or other deciduous trees; California milkmaids is one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom in California's oak woodlands, often flowering by midwinter, and goes dormant with the arrival of summer drought.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions or fall-sown seed in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade under oaks or other deciduous trees; California milkmaids is one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom in the state's oak woodlands, often flowering by midwinter, and disappears with the onset of summer drought like other toothworts. Cardamine californica produces compound, toothed leaves and slender stems bearing loose clusters of white to pale lavender-pink, four-petaled flowers that appear from December through April depending on elevation and rainfall, brightening the winter woodland floor well before most other perennials stir. Common under oaks and in mixed evergreen forest from the Coast Ranges into the Sierra Nevada foothills, it is well adapted to a summer-dry, winter-wet Mediterranean climate and needs no irrigation once dormant. Plant beneath deciduous oaks alongside other winter- and spring-blooming California natives such as trillium and hound's tongue, and allow the foliage to die back naturally after seed is set.

common_name: Nuttall's Toothwort (Slender Toothwort of the Pacific Northwest)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; Nuttall's toothwort blooms very early in Pacific Northwest woodlands and dies back to its slender rhizomes by early summer.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; Nuttall's toothwort is among the first wildflowers to bloom in Pacific Northwest lowland forests, often flowering in February and March, and dies back to its slender, tooth-shaped rhizomes by early summer. Cardamine nuttallii bears finely divided, delicate leaves and short stems carrying a few pale pink to white four-petaled flowers, smaller and more diminutive overall than its eastern relatives, and is easily overlooked in the leaf litter until its blooms open. Native from British Columbia south through Washington and Oregon into northern California, it favors humus-rich soil in mixed conifer-broadleaf forest and along shaded woodland edges. Plant in drifts with trillium, fawn lily, and other Pacific Northwest spring ephemerals for a fleeting but rewarding early-season display, and avoid disturbing the site through summer while the plant is dormant underground.
